2.text: be found trespassing in Russian waters or carrying on unlawful trade on the

3.text: shores. I cannot tell whether the “Kreisser” seized any American ships or

4.text: not, though several of them have been taken at different periods; but she

5.text: met the schooner “Henrietta,” just bought by Kuvaˊr, and carried her off as

6.text: a prize, in spite of all remonstrance. The schooner was afterwards fitted with

7.text: a steam-engine and used for keeping watch on the Sea of Okhotsk, where

8.text: she was lost in a storm in 1895. Kuvaˊr applied several times to the authori-

9.text: ties for redress, but without avail. The officials in Vladivostok maintained

10.text: that the schooner was not yet paid for; but I was told at Indian Point that

11.text: Kuvaˊr gave for it the whalebone of two whales, a large pile of walrus-tusks,

12.text: three bagfuls of white-fox skins, and three polar-bear skins. During my stay,

13.text: another occasion to buy a schooner presented itself, and I was asked for

14.text: advice as to the possibility of a second confiscation, but withheld my opinion.

15.text: American wares generally are twice as cheap as those brought from the

16.text: interior of Siberia. Even those brought from Vladivostok by sea cannot

17.text: compete with them, because most of them are of American origin, and have

18.text: come by a more circuitous route. American granulated sugar forms an exception.

19.text: It is inferior to the well-refined, hard lump-sugar of the Russians. American

20.text: cutlery is not always so well adapted to the uses of the natives as are the

21.text: rough strong knives made for this purpose in Yakutsk, Sredne-Kolymsk, Mar-

22.text: kova, etc. Moreover, the whalers do not trade in brick-tea, because they do

23.text: not visit any Chinese or southern Siberian ports. Once or twice they brought

24.text: brick-tea from Japan; but Japanese brick-tea is of much poorer quality than

25.text: Chinese, and the cakes are smaller in size.

26.text: After the native stock of whalebone became exhausted, the whalers began

27.text: to accept instead walrus ivory and the skins of white foxes and of black and

28.text: polar bears. Other Asiatic peltries, such as those of red and cross foxes and

29.text: of wolves, also skins from America, like the beaver and marten, are taken to

30.text: the Russian fairs because they fetch a much better price in Asia than would

31.text: be paid by the whalers. At the present time the chief source of income of

32.text: the natives are fawn-skins, which are much needed by the American natives

33.text: and by the Alaskan miners for making garments; also skins of full-grown

34.text: reindeer for sleeping-bags, ready-made garments even of poor quality, and,

35.text: most of all, various kinds of seal-skin boots, which are used both by the

36.text: whaling-crews and by the miners. Asiatic and American natives sell these

37.text: boots by the thousand every summer; but the demand keeps increasing, and

38.text: in 1901 the price at Indian Point was a sack of flour per pair.

39.text: The chief places for trade continue to be East Cape, and especially Indian

40.text: Point, where the sea is cleared of ice by the strong currents as early as the

41.text: middle of April. Two or three native traders in both places have acquired

42.text: year by year a larger amount of native products, until finally they are able

43.text: to obtain by exchange each summer a sufficient amount of European wares
